message.content:
Black holes form when **gravity overwhelms pressure** in an object, causing it to collapse into an extremely dense region from which not even light can escape.[1][2] The most common way this happens is when a **massive star** runs out of fuel, its core collapses, and—if the remaining core is massive enough after the supernova—becomes a black hole.[2][6][9]

A simple breakdown:

- A massive star spends its life fusing elements in its core to produce energy.[2]
- Once the star can no longer fuse elements efficiently, the outward pressure drops.[2]
- The core collapses under its own gravity; the outer layers may be blown off in a **supernova**.[2][6]
- If the leftover core is sufficiently massive, collapse continues until an event horizon forms, creating a black hole.[2][4]

There are also other proposed formation paths:

- **Mergers** of neutron stars or black holes can produce a black hole.[1][6]
- **Supermassive black holes** may form by repeated mergers, rapid gas accretion, or direct collapse of large gas clouds.[1][4][6]
- **Primordial black holes** are a theoretical possibility from very early-universe density fluctuations, but they have not been conclusively detected.[1][6]

If you want, I can also explain **what happens inside a star right before it becomes a black hole** or **why light can’t escape one**.
